c.text: Chapter 9 – Burnout and Boundaries
Notice strain before it becomes a crisis
Leaders do not usually collapse in a dramatic way.
They erode.

It looks like this. You start dreading Sunday morning slightly. You notice you are short with your children on the drive home. A volunteer cancels and your reaction is disproportionate. Prayer feels like paperwork. You find yourself thinking that you would be relieved if the whole thing quietly ended.
These signs deserve attention, whether they have lasted weeks or months. They do not diagnose a condition, but they can signal that your workload, support or health needs care.
The most sobering part is that this happens to leaders who are doing everything right. Burnout is not the punishment for laziness. It is usually what happens to the conscientious.
Elijah after Mount Carmel
1 Kings 18 ends with Elijah’s triumph on Mount Carmel – fire from heaven, the prophets of Baal defeated, rain returning after three years of drought, Elijah running ahead of Ahab’s chariot.

After the events at Mount Carmel, 1 Kings 19 describes Jezebel threatening Elijah’s life within twenty-four hours. Elijah flees into the wilderness, sits beneath a broom tree and asks God to take his life. The account does not specify that all this happened the very next day.
Look at what God does, and the order of it.
First, sleep.
Verse 5: he lay down and slept.
Second, food.
An angel touches him, and there is bread and a jar of water. He eats and lies down again. The angel comes a second time and says the journey is too much for him.
Third, more sleep and more food.
Only after all of that does the journey to Horeb happen.
Then, presence.
At Horeb there is wind, earthquake and fire, and God is not in any of them – and then the low whisper of verse 12.
Then, a wider perspective.
Elijah says he alone is left. God tells him that seven thousand in Israel have not bowed to Baal. Elijah’s distress is real, but he does not know the whole picture.
Finally, a colleague.
God tells him to anoint Elisha to succeed him. The answer to Elijah’s exhaustion included another person.
Sleep, food, presence, truth, and company.

If you are running on empty, that is not a bad order to work through – and notice how physical the first half of it is. God did not begin with a rebuke or a Bible study. He let his prophet sleep and fed him twice.
Jesus told his team to stop

Mark 6:30-31 comes right after the disciples return from their mission. They report everything, and Jesus tells them to come with him by themselves to a quiet place and get some rest. Mark adds the reason: so many people were coming and going that they did not even have a chance to eat.
The demand was real, the ministry was fruitful, and Jesus called a halt. Rest was his instruction, not their indulgence.

And the Sabbath itself is not a productivity technique. Genesis 2:2-3 grounds it in creation – God rested on the seventh day and made it holy – and Exodus 20:8-11 builds the fourth commandment on that pattern. Rest is written into how the world is made. Ignoring it is not extra devotion; it is a quiet claim that the work depends on you.
Psalm 127:1-2 says it more sharply.
Unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labour in vain. It is in vain to rise early and stay up late, eating the bread of anxious toil – for he gives sleep to those he loves.
The bill your family is paying

1 Timothy 3:4-5 is uncomfortable and necessary. Among the qualifications for an overseer, Paul says he must manage his own household well – and then asks directly: if anyone does not know how to manage his own family, how can he take care of God’s church?
Paul makes the home the qualifying ground, not the leftover.

This is the area where new leaders do the most damage without noticing, because ministry provides such excellent cover. Nobody criticises you for missing dinner to visit a sick member. Your children are not able to compete with a good cause, so they stop trying.
Some honest questions to sit with:
Does your family get your best hours or your leftover ones?
Would your spouse say your ministry has been good for your marriage over the past year?
Have any of your children come to experience church as the thing that repeatedly takes their parent away?

And a harder one: is any part of you using ministry to avoid something at home? Ministry is a socially applauded way to be absent. If home is difficult, the church can become the place where you feel competent and appreciated, and the escape can look exactly like devotion.
If that question landed somewhere, that is worth talking to someone about this month.
Learning to say no
Most overload is not one huge commitment.
It is fifteen small yeses given in corridors.
Three practical rules.
Pause before accepting a new commitment.

“Let me check my calendar and the commitments this would affect. I’ll come back to you tomorrow.” If you share a household, involve those affected. You do not need a spouse to have limits worth respecting.
Decide what your capacity actually is, in advance.
Write down the hours you can give in a normal week. When something new comes, ask what it replaces. If nothing can come off, the answer is no – and that is a full answer.
Say no to good things.

In Mark 1:36-38, after Jesus’ early-morning prayer, the disciples find him and tell him everyone is looking for him. He replies that they should go somewhere else, to the nearby villages, so he can preach there too – because that is why he came. Luke 4:42-43 records the crowd trying to keep him from leaving, and he goes anyway.
There were still sick people in Capernaum when he left.
Jesus did not meet every need in front of him, because he knew which work was his.
You will not either. That is not failure; it is having a calling rather than a compulsion.
What to actually put in place
One protected day a week.
Same day where possible, phone away, family knows it, team knows it. Take it even when you feel fine – especially then.
A finishing time on ministry evenings.
Meetings end when you said they would (Chapter 6) partly for your own sake.
A quarterly conversation with your spouse, family member or trusted friend about the effect of ministry on your life. Ask what they notice, rather than offering only a report about the work.
A break each year that is longer than a weekend.
Arrange cover in advance rather than hoping for a quiet fortnight.
The monthly person from Chapter 2, with permission to ask how you are actually doing.
Look after the body.
Sleep, food, and some walking are spiritual disciplines in disguise. God started there with Elijah.
When it is more than tiredness
Be honest with yourself about the difference between being tired and being unwell.

If the flatness does not lift after rest, if you have lost interest in things you used to enjoy, if you are not sleeping or are sleeping constantly, if you feel hopeless about things generally rather than just about the ministry – that is worth taking to a doctor, not just to a prayer meeting. Seeing a professional is not a lack of faith, any more than setting a broken arm is.

If you are thinking about suicide or harming yourself, seek urgent help rather than waiting for rest to work. If there is immediate danger or you cannot stay safe, contact local emergency services or go to an emergency department. Tell a trusted person who can stay with you while help is arranged. Tell someone you trust and ask about reducing or pausing responsibilities. Recovery deserves time and support whether or not you return to the same role. Your worth is not measured by your usefulness to a church.

Matthew 11:28-30 is Jesus’ invitation to all who are weary and burdened, to take his yoke and find rest, because his yoke is easy and his burden is light. A yoke is still work – but if what you are carrying feels nothing like that description, it is worth asking how much of the weight he actually gave you.
